title: A 31-year AMO lag gave no forecast skill for Florida loggerhead nesting in 2010-2025; only the previous-December sea temperature term kept skill, and neither term transferred to South Carolina
abstract: Question: does the published climate model of Van Houtan and Halley (2011) forecast loggerhead turtle nest counts after its fit period? The model uses the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) lagged 31 years and the sea surface temperature (SST) of the previous December. With this lag, the AMO input for 2010-2025 was known in 2011, so the 16 later seasons give a clean test. Data: annual nests on 27 core Florida index beaches (1989-2025) and on 6 South Carolina index beaches (1982-2025), digitized from agency charts (error below 0.6% per year), with the NOAA Kaplan AMO and ERSST v5. Method: we fitted the four published model forms on the years before 2010 and forecast 2010-2025 with observed inputs. We compared the forecasts with simple baselines, with 2,000 spectrum-matched random AMO series and with an SST-only model. Results: in Florida, AMO-only models did not beat the fit-period mean (MSE ratios 1.32 and 1.02). Adding the AMO terms to the SST-only model increased the error (ratio 1.08 to 1.26). For the full model, 3.4% of random AMO series fitted 1989-2009 as well as the real AMO (R 0.74), and 20% forecast equally well or better. Only the December SST term kept skill: the SST-only model cut the forecast MSE by 50% (sign-flip p 0.0025; random-SST p 0.0035). Its detrended slope was 0.17 +/- 0.12 ln nests per C in 1989-2009 and 0.11 +/- 0.07 in 2010-2025. In South Carolina, no AMO model fitted or forecast better than the mean, the December SST slope was near zero in each period, and nests increased 0.52 ln per decade after 2010 without a model prediction. The best AMO lag changed from 31 to 21-39 years with the data set. Limitations: digitized series, 27 instead of the original 15 Florida beaches, model form read from text, 16 test years, no Japan test, and a fixed May-August count window.

Lines show model fits before 2010 and forecasts for 2010-2025 (grey area) with observed inputs. The AMO models do not forecast better than the fit-period mean; the previous-December SST model does in Florida only.

Florida model M4 with the real AMO (black line) and with 2,000 random AMO series that have the same power spectrum (bars). Left: in-sample R for 1989-2009. Right: forecast RMSE of ln nests for 2010-2025; 20% of random series forecast equally well or better.

Detrended ln nests against detrended previous-December SST (22-38N, 72-84W) for the fit and test periods in Florida and South Carolina, and the AICc profile of the AMO lag. The Florida slope is similar in both periods; the South Carolina slope is near zero. The best lag is not 31 years.
